paragraphs: Comparing several learning algorithms often involves an overall statistical test followed by comparisons between individual pairs. This paper develops a Bayesian alternative to that workflow. It uses a Dirichlet process prior to construct a nonparametric counterpart of the Friedman test, framing algorithm comparison through posterior probabilities rather than only significance tests and p-values.

The analysis also gives a geometric interpretation of the conventional Friedman test: from the proposed Bayesian perspective, it concerns a multivariate mean and whether an ellipsoid is included in a relevant region. For multiple comparisons, the authors develop a joint procedure that accounts for dependencies between comparisons instead of treating each comparison as an isolated inference.

A stated benefit is the ability to assess support for the null hypothesis, beyond merely rejecting it. The authors also apply the procedure to algorithm racing, where the task is to identify the best candidate from a large collection. Simulations show competitive accuracy and speed for that selection task, supporting the approach as a practical comparison procedure.
icml-2015-a-bayesian-nonparametric-proce.tldr: A Bayesian approach jointly compares algorithms, accounts for dependent comparisons, and shows competitive performance in selecting the best candidate.

paragraphs: In a two-player zero-sum stochastic game, learning a good strategy requires accounting for an opponent whose interests conflict with yours. This paper studies what happens when dynamic programming calculations for such games are approximate. Its central question is how errors in intermediate computations affect the quality of the strategy ultimately obtained.

The authors give a unified error analysis for approximate value iteration, policy iteration, and generalized policy iteration adapted to stochastic games. The analysis uses Lp norms and distinguishes errors in estimating values from errors in the approximate greedy operation. It bounds the suboptimality of an achievable stationary policy in terms of both errors and the discount factor.

The paper also introduces AGPI-Q, a practical batch algorithm for infinite-horizon discounted games. It extends the Fitted-Q approach from Markov decision processes to the two-player setting and permits a nonparametric implementation. Experiments on the simultaneous game Alesia demonstrate its performance, connecting the theoretical treatment of approximation errors to an implemented game-solving method.
icml-2015-approximate-dynamic-programmin.tldr: The paper bounds approximation-error propagation in two-player zero-sum games and introduces a batch learning algorithm called AGPI-Q.

paragraphs: Working set methods accelerate optimization by repeatedly solving smaller pieces of a larger problem. Their practical success leaves important choices unresolved: how large each subproblem should be, which variables it should contain, and when to stop solving it. This paper introduces Blitz to give these choices a stronger theoretical foundation.

The main result connects subproblem size with progress toward convergence without imposing assumptions on the data. That relationship motivates ways to tune the algorithm's parameters and discard variables that become irrelevant as optimization proceeds. The smaller problems therefore serve a measurable purpose in solving the full problem, rather than being selected solely through implementation heuristics.

Applied to L1-regularized learning, Blitz is reported to outperform existing solvers in sequential execution, settings with limited memory, and distributed computation. Those results show that the approach can help under several different resource constraints. The framework is also broader than that particular regularizer, making it relevant to other optimization applications involving sparsity or constraints.
icml-2015-blitz-a-principled-meta-algori.tldr: Blitz connects working-set size to convergence progress, guiding faster sparse optimization across several computing settings.

paragraphs: Detecting an event in a long Internet video is difficult because only a few shots may actually show relevant evidence. Other shots can be unrelated or misleading. This paper addresses that imbalance by making the relevance of individual shots part of the detector, instead of pooling all shots without regard to their usefulness.

The method assigns each shot a semantic saliency score describing its relevance to the event of interest. It orders shots by these scores, reflecting the expectation that more relevant shots should contribute more to the final decision. A new isotonic regularizer incorporates this ordering into a support vector machine, producing the proposed nearly-isotonic SVM classifier.

The authors develop an efficient implementation based on proximal gradient optimization and derive closed-form proximal steps for the method. Experiments on three real-world video datasets support the effectiveness of the overall approach. The contribution joins a way to identify useful evidence within long videos with a classifier designed to exploit that evidence's ordering.
icml-2015-complex-event-detection-using-.tldr: Semantic shot rankings guide a nearly-isotonic SVM to improve complex-event detection in long videos.

paragraphs: This paper studies regression problems whose coefficients form a tensor, a multidimensional arrangement of parameters. The setting appears in collaborative filtering, multi-task learning, and analysis of data varying across space and time. The authors investigate how quickly a Bayesian estimator learns when that coefficient tensor has a low-rank structure.

The analysis covers predictive accuracy both on the observed inputs and on new inputs. It establishes a fast learning rate without requiring strong convexity of the observation. It also shows adaptation to an unknown true rank: the estimator can achieve a nearly optimal rate that depends on that rank even when the rank is not supplied beforehand.

To judge how strong this result is, the authors derive a minimax learning rate for the tensor-estimation problem. This provides a benchmark for the best achievable worst-case statistical performance. Comparing the Bayesian estimator's bound with that benchmark shows that the bound is tight and the estimator is near minimax optimal, rather than merely statistically consistent.
icml-2015-convergence-rate-of-bayesian-t.tldr: A Bayesian low-rank tensor estimator achieves fast, rank-adaptive prediction rates that are near minimax optimal.

paragraphs: Context trees represent conditional probability patterns in which some dependencies disappear in particular contexts. Parsimonious context trees offer more structural flexibility, which can make learning statistically more efficient when data are scarce. Their drawback is expensive structure learning: the existing procedure is practical only with small alphabets and shallow trees.

This paper asks how much flexibility can be retained while keeping learning computationally feasible. It pursues two complementary routes. One improves the algorithm used to learn parsimonious context trees. The other develops related generalizations of ordinary context trees that deliberately surrender some structural flexibility in exchange for easier computation.

Experiments on simulated and real-world data show substantial improvement when these routes are combined. The result matters because statistical efficiency and computational efficiency are separate requirements: a model that uses limited observations well still needs a tractable learning procedure. The paper's approach addresses both through changes to the learning algorithm and to the family of structures it searches.
icml-2015-dealing-with-small-data-on-the.tldr: Improved learning algorithms and selectively flexible tree structures make context-tree generalizations more practical for small datasets.

paragraphs: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo relies on numerically solving differential equations to propose new samples. The quality of that numerical integration directly affects sampling efficiency. This paper focuses on stiff equations with rapidly oscillating components, which the usual leapfrog integrator can struggle to reproduce even with carefully chosen parameters and preconditioning.

The proposed exponential integrator uses a Gaussian approximation to separate out stiff components of the dynamics. It integrates that part analytically for stability, then uses variation of constants to account for departures from the approximation. This makes the Gaussian approximation a tool for organizing the numerical calculation while retaining a treatment of the remaining dynamics.

The authors explore several ways to obtain the Gaussian approximation and evaluate exponential HMC on benchmark learning problems. Comparisons with methods for improving leapfrog HMC show advantages in producing effective samples, maintaining high acceptance rates, and keeping runtime short. These are empirical findings about the studied problems, supporting the value of changing the integration method itself.
icml-2015-exponential-integration-for-ha.tldr: Exponential HMC analytically handles stiff dynamics identified through a Gaussian approximation, improving sampling efficiency in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Cover trees organize data to accelerate exact nearest-neighbor searches in arbitrary metric spaces. This paper improves their structure and implementation while retaining that exact-search purpose. The contribution combines a simpler tree definition, a new structural invariant, parallel algorithms, and a memory layout designed to use the cache more efficiently.

The revised definition gives a tree with exactly one node per data point, replacing an earlier linear-order node count with an exact count of n. The additional invariant helps queries run faster in practice. Parallel construction and querying exploit multiprocessor systems, while the memory-layout change addresses the cost of accessing the tree during computation.

The reported benchmarks show 10–50% fewer distance computations on standard datasets and 71% fewer on a large bioinformatics dataset. On a large image dataset, construction using 16 cores takes 12 minutes instead of 3.5 hours. These results demonstrate gains in both search work and construction time, with each numerical improvement tied to its stated evaluation setting.
icml-2015-faster-cover-trees-ea3b85e5d2.tldr: Structural, parallel, and memory-layout improvements make cover trees faster to construct and query while preserving exact nearest-neighbor search.

paragraphs: Some observations naturally occupy curved spaces, so a statistical model needs to respect that geometry. Many existing parametric models on manifolds work within a small neighborhood because their geometric ingredients are locally defined. This paper addresses the resulting difficulty of describing observations that extend beyond a single local region.

The proposed framework combines multivariate general linear models across multiple tangent spaces. Each local model handles a neighborhood, and their mixture extends the description across the manifold. The authors formulate this as a Dirichlet process mixture, providing a nonparametric framework that generalizes existing linear-model approaches in both Euclidean and non-Euclidean settings.

Grouping observations into subpopulations also exposes hidden geometric structure. In particular, the framework is intended to discover geodesic relationships between covariates and responses that lie on a manifold. Proof-of-concept experiments validate the model. The main contribution is therefore a recipe for combining locally meaningful statistical relationships into a broader model, together with an initial demonstration of that recipe.
icml-2015-manifold-valued-dirichlet-proc.tldr: A Dirichlet process mixture combines local linear models across tangent spaces to model manifold-valued responses beyond a single neighborhood.

paragraphs: This paper combines variational Bayesian inference with Markov chain Monte Carlo. The starting point is an advance in stochastic gradient variational inference: posterior approximations can contain auxiliary random variables. That additional flexibility allows the approximation to include a sampling procedure as part of its construction, expanding the kinds of distributions the method can represent.

The authors incorporate one or more MCMC steps directly into the variational approximation. The resulting algorithms still optimize an explicit objective, preserving a central practical feature of variational methods. At the same time, the sampling steps provide a way to spend additional computation on improving the posterior approximation.

The contribution is a family of inference algorithms with an adjustable tradeoff between computational effort and accuracy. The paper develops the theoretical foundations for this combination and presents promising initial results. Its stated evidence supports the feasibility and potential of the synthesis, while the main conceptual advance is making iterative sampling compatible with an explicitly optimized variational approximation.
icml-2015-markov-chain-monte-carlo-and-v.tldr: Embedding MCMC steps inside variational approximations creates inference algorithms that trade additional computation for additional accuracy.

paragraphs: Relational models often organize interactions into blocks, allowing different groups of entities to have different patterns of connection. Mondrian processes make these block structures flexible, but that flexibility can encourage overfitting when observations are sparse. This paper uses associated metadata, such as user profiles, to guide the model's organization.

The metadata dependent Mondrian process incorporates this information in two places: the random partition of the product space and the allocation of entities to the resulting blocks. It encourages blocks whose relational interactions are similar while also discouraging excessive diversity in their metadata labels. Metadata therefore helps regularize how the block structure is formed and populated.

The authors report greater robustness under data sparsity and easier convergence of posterior inference. In link-prediction and rating-prediction applications, the method achieves higher prediction accuracy than the evaluated baseline models while using a more parsimonious structure. These findings support using entity information to constrain flexible relational models when observed interactions alone provide limited guidance.
icml-2015-metadata-dependent-mondrian-pr.tldr: Metadata guides Mondrian partitions and entity assignments, improving sparse relational prediction with more parsimonious block structures.

paragraphs: Subspace segmentation clusters points assumed to lie in several linear or affine subspaces. A successful approach represents each point sparsely using the other points, then converts those representations into similarities for spectral clustering. The guiding idea is that a sparse representation should draw its nonzero coefficients from points in the same subspace.

The paper identifies two problems with computing each representation independently using L1 minimization. The available dictionary is built from the data and can have strong structure, undermining favorable properties associated with randomized dictionaries. Independent fitting also ignores useful relationships among the points that could inform the representations jointly.

The authors propose a multi-task learning framework that couples these sparse representations. Its design addresses correlation structure while tailoring the representations to produce an affinity matrix suited to segmentation. Theoretical analysis and empirical tests support the claims. The methodological shift is to treat representation learning across points as a connected problem whose output serves the final clustering stage.
icml-2015-multi-task-learning-for-subspa.tldr: Jointly learning sparse representations helps subspace segmentation handle correlated data and build a better clustering affinity matrix.

paragraphs: Sequential Monte Carlo samples from a sequence of probability distributions. This paper extends that framework to support complex models with high-dimensional random variables through nested sequential Monte Carlo. The key change concerns how proposal samples are generated: they may be approximate, provided they carry the proper weights required by the method.

Under that weighting requirement, the outer procedure remains a correct SMC algorithm. An NSMC sampler can itself produce the properly weighted samples needed by another sampler, so the construction can be repeated through multiple levels. This recursive property lets an inner sampling procedure construct a high-dimensional proposal for an outer one.

The importance of the result is that approximate internal sampling can fit within a formally valid overall procedure when its weighting is handled correctly. The authors demonstrate results on filtering problems with dimensions on the order of 100 to 1000. Those examples motivate the approach's effectiveness for demanding filtering tasks, alongside the general framework permitting arbitrary nesting depth.
icml-2015-nested-sequential-monte-carlo-.tldr: Nested SMC uses properly weighted approximate proposals, allowing samplers to be composed recursively for high-dimensional inference.

paragraphs: This paper develops discriminative factor analysis for observations that need not be Gaussian. Its Bayesian model uses the ranks of the data, making relative ordering central to the observation model. The first contribution is a max-margin version of the rank-likelihood, which brings a margin-based principle into the modeling of those ordered observations.

The authors combine that likelihood with linear Bayesian support vector machines to create a discriminative factor model. Both components use a max-margin principle, linking the treatment of observations with the classification component. They then extend the classifier to nonlinear behavior by using a Dirichlet process mixture of local linear classifiers.

The model retains local conjugacy, enabling efficient inference through either Markov chain Monte Carlo or variational Bayes. Experiments on benchmark and real data report superior performance and suggest potential applications in computational biology. The contribution brings together rank-based modeling, discriminative factors, and flexible classification while maintaining inference procedures that the authors describe as computationally efficient.
icml-2015-non-gaussian-discriminative-fa.tldr: A rank-based Bayesian factor model combines max-margin observation modeling with linear or nonlinear classification for non-Gaussian data.

paragraphs: Cross-domain collaborative filtering uses rating information from several domains to improve recommendations. Its usefulness depends on what relationships a model can transfer between those domains. This paper argues that existing approaches based on sharing substructures are limited to transferring knowledge with linear correlations, leaving nonlinear relationships outside their representational scope.

The proposed Hyper-Structure Transfer approach introduces a more complex structure shared across all domains. Each domain's rating matrix must be explainable as a projection of that common structure. Sharing happens through this underlying object, allowing the model to identify and transfer relationships that are nonlinearly correlated across the observed rating matrices.

This changes the form of the connection imposed between domains: the common explanation can be richer than a directly shared substructure. The authors conduct extensive experiments and report empirical evidence that their HST models are effective. The stated contribution is therefore both a modeling proposal for nonlinear knowledge transfer and an experimental demonstration of its usefulness for cross-domain recommendation.
icml-2015-non-linear-cross-domain-collab.tldr: Hyper-Structure Transfer connects rating matrices through a shared complex structure to transfer nonlinear relationships across recommendation domains.

paragraphs: Greedy selection is widely used for submodular maximization, including sensor-selection tasks based on entropy or mutual information. Standard theory provides a 1 − 1/e approximation guarantee, yet practical solutions often appear much closer to optimal. This paper investigates why the general guarantee can substantially understate the quality observed in those applications.

The authors analyze the curvature of entropy and mutual-information objectives built using Gaussian RBF kernels. Curvature supplies information about the particular objective beyond its broad classification as submodular. Examining that additional structure gives a route to understanding why greedy choices can be especially effective for the objectives under study.

The result is a theoretical justification for a nearly optimal approximation ratio in the analyzed setting. Its significance lies in connecting strong practical behavior to properties of the objective itself. The explanation is specifically grounded in the curvature analysis for Gaussian RBF kernels, so the paper's claim concerns that structured setting rather than every possible submodular maximization problem.
icml-2015-on-greedy-maximization-of-entr.tldr: Curvature analysis of entropy and mutual-information objectives with Gaussian RBF kernels helps explain nearly optimal greedy selection.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to identify the best option, or a group of top options, when observations are noisy and arrive through selectable subsets. At each round, the learner chooses from an available family of subsets and receives information about the options in that subset. The goal is reliable identification using as few measurements as possible.

The setting generalizes best-arm identification by making the structure of the available feedback part of the problem. The authors develop algorithms that exploit this combinatorial structure in a substantive way. They also establish that the algorithms cannot be improved in certain special cases, giving a qualified optimality result for those cases.

The algorithms rely on a set multi-covering oracle, which handles an associated combinatorial selection problem. Their efficiency and performance therefore depend strongly on whether that problem can be solved efficiently. This dependence is central to the contribution: structured feedback offers opportunities to economize on measurements, but realizing those opportunities also requires solving the accompanying subset-selection problem.
icml-2015-on-identifying-good-options-un.tldr: Algorithms exploit structured subset feedback to identify high-quality options efficiently, with performance tied to a set multi-covering oracle.

paragraphs: In a multiple-play bandit problem, a learner selects several arms in each round rather than just one. This paper extends Thompson sampling to that setting through an algorithm called MP-TS. The motivation is to carry a randomized, Bayesian-inspired approach with strong single-play results into a problem requiring several simultaneous selections.

The main theoretical result is a regret upper bound matching the established lower bound for the problem. This establishes optimal regret for MP-TS in the studied setting. The authors identify it as the first computationally efficient algorithm with this optimality property, combining a statistical guarantee with a method intended to be practical to run.

Computer simulations compare MP-TS with state-of-the-art algorithms. The paper also introduces a modified version that performs better empirically. These contributions have distinct roles: the regret analysis establishes the stated optimality of MP-TS, while the simulation findings motivate the modification as a practical improvement without presenting that empirical gain as a separate universal guarantee.
icml-2015-optimal-regret-analysis-of-tho.tldr: Multiple-play Thompson sampling achieves an optimal regret bound, and a proposed modification improves empirical performance.

paragraphs: Binary matrix factorization can uncover overlapping groups in network data, allowing entities to belong to more than one group. Applying these models to large networks creates an inference challenge. Existing techniques may be computationally expensive or lack a way to select the model's structure, restricting their usefulness as network size grows.

The paper proposes stochastic factorized asymptotic Bayesian inference, abbreviated sFAB. It combines ideas from stochastic variational inference and factorized asymptotic Bayesian inference. The resulting framework is designed to offer scalability and inherent model selection together, addressing both the cost of fitting a relational model and the choice of its complexity.

Empirical comparisons report better accuracy and scalability for sFAB with binary matrix factorization than for state-of-the-art inference methods for overlapping relational models. The contribution matters because discovering overlapping network structure requires more than a representationally suitable model. The authors provide an inference approach that can also make model-selection decisions while handling large-scale data efficiently.
icml-2015-scalable-model-selection-for-l.tldr: sFAB combines scalable inference and model selection for binary matrix factorization, improving reported accuracy and scalability on relational data.

paragraphs: With infinitely many bandit arms, a learner cannot try every available option, even once. A finite sampling budget must therefore be divided among a limited selection of arms. This paper focuses on simple regret: the quality of the option ultimately selected, rather than the accumulated cost of choices made during exploration.

The proposed algorithm targets that final-selection objective. Its rate depends on a parameter, beta, describing the distribution of near-optimal arms. This dependence captures a fundamental feature of the setting: the difficulty of finding an excellent option changes with how those options are distributed. Depending on beta, the authors prove minimax optimality up to either a constant multiplier or a logarithmic factor.

The paper also extends the approach to cases where beta is unknown, where near-optimal arms naturally have small variance, and where the time horizon is unknown. These extensions broaden the situations covered by the method. The contribution establishes a theoretically grounded treatment of final recommendation quality in an exploration space too large to exhaust.
icml-2015-simple-regret-for-infinitely-m.tldr: An infinite-armed bandit algorithm targets final-choice quality with minimax guarantees that depend on the distribution of near-optimal arms.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes offer flexible models, but their cubic computational complexity creates a scaling problem. Sparse methods address this by concentrating computation on a smaller collection of pseudo-samples. This paper extends that strategy beyond Gaussian observation likelihoods, aiming to preserve sparse inference when the form of the observed data calls for other likelihoods.

The authors derive a variational sparse solution using a new expression for the gradients needed during inference. Those gradients are characterized through individual observation likelihood terms. They also propose optimizing the sparse approximation through a fixed-point computation, giving the approach a concrete iterative procedure for finding the approximation.

Experiments show that the fixed-point operator behaves as a contraction in many cases, which leads to rapid convergence in those cases. Evaluations on count regression, classification, and ordinal regression illustrate the breadth and advantages of the method. The stated convergence evidence is empirical and qualified, while the broader contribution is a sparse variational framework for generalized GP observation models.
icml-2015-sparse-variational-inference-f.tldr: A sparse variational GP method supports general likelihoods and uses fixed-point optimization that converges quickly in many tested cases.

paragraphs: Approximate Message Passing can recover signals from noisy measurements that contain fewer dimensions than the original signal. It offers strong reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency, but its iterations can fail to converge when a problem does not closely match its assumptions. This paper targets that instability without abandoning the AMP approach.

The proposed change concerns the update schedule. Standard AMP updates coefficients in parallel, whereas the swept version applies updates to individual coefficients. The authors show that this modification can stabilize problems on which the standard iteration diverges. In those cases, it makes theoretically expected reconstruction performance attainable when the original iteration could not deliver it.

The paper also examines whether the altered schedule imposes an excessive computational cost. Its results indicate that the added burden is manageable, allowing efficient application to high-dimensional signals. The contribution is therefore a practical change to the iteration that can recover AMP's expected benefits in difficult settings while retaining useful computational efficiency.
icml-2015-swept-approximate-message-pass.tldr: Updating AMP coefficients individually can stabilize otherwise divergent problems while keeping high-dimensional signal recovery computationally practical.

paragraphs: Tasks such as exemplar clustering, document summarization, and sensor placement can be formulated as constrained submodular maximization. On massive datasets, the resulting optimization may exceed what one machine can handle. This paper develops a distributed greedy approach intended to retain useful solution quality while spreading the computation across machines.

The algorithm combines previous approaches with randomization. The resulting computation is highly amenable to parallel execution, and the authors prove a constant-factor approximation guarantee in the worst case. This guarantee gives a formal quality bound for the distributed procedure, complementing its ability to divide a large optimization problem into parallel work.

Experiments examine large problems under different kinds of constraints. They demonstrate efficiency and obtain objective values consistently close to those achievable in the centralized setting in the reported evaluations. The theoretical and experimental findings address different concerns: the former bounds worst-case quality, while the latter shows that distributing the work can preserve much of the centralized solution quality in practice.
icml-2015-the-power-of-randomization-dis.tldr: Randomized distributed greedy optimization provides constant-factor guarantees and achieves near-centralized objective values in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: A value function estimates the long-term reward associated with a state. This paper adds the goal as an explicit input, creating a universal value function approximator that can generalize across both states and goals. One shared model can therefore express how the value of a state changes with the objective being pursued.

The authors develop an efficient supervised-learning method by factoring observed values into separate state and goal embeddings. They then learn mappings from states and goals to those embedding vectors. This separates the representation of where the agent is from the representation of what it is trying to accomplish, while learning from their combined effect on value.

The paper shows how to incorporate the technique into reinforcement learning so that observed rewards alone drive the value-function updates. It also demonstrates successful generalization to previously unseen goals. That finding supports the central proposal: sharing a value approximation across goals can carry learned information into objectives that were not previously encountered.
icml-2015-universal-value-function-appro.tldr: Universal value function approximators learn shared state-and-goal representations and demonstrate generalization to previously unseen goals.

paragraphs: A model may have abundant labeled examples from one domain but no labels from the domain where it will be used. This paper proposes a deep-learning adaptation method that trains on labeled source data and unlabeled target data. Its aim is to make the learned representation useful despite the shift between those domains.

Training encourages features with two properties: they distinguish the main task's classes in the source domain, and they are invariant to the domain shift. The authors achieve this by adding a few standard layers and a gradient reversal layer. The augmented network can be trained with ordinary backpropagation and applied to almost any feed-forward architecture.

Image-classification experiments show an adaptation effect even with large domain shifts, and the method outperforms previous state-of-the-art results on the Office datasets. Its practical appeal combines the absence of a target-label requirement with a relatively simple architectural modification. The findings support learning transferable features through the training objective and network structure rather than requiring labeled target examples.
icml-2015-unsupervised-domain-adaptation.tldr: A gradient reversal layer helps networks learn task-discriminative, domain-invariant features using labeled source data and unlabeled target data.
